source.title: Multi-Game Decision Transformers
source.authors: Ian S. Fischer; Daniel Freeman; S. Guadarrama; Eric Jang; Kuang-Huei Lee; L. Lee; H. Michalewski; Igor Mordatch; Ofir Nachum; Winnie Xu; Mengjiao Yang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether downstream task performance changes with model size, using Atari game scores rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws and reports scaling of Atari performance, not held-out loss, power-law fits, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Only the reported Atari performance scaling results bear on V6. The scaling plots give no numeric point values; the text describes their trends. Other performance comparisons and the expert-action inference results do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper motivates itself with language-model scaling laws and reports that Atari game score rises with model size for offline RL agents. It fits no power law and measures no held-out loss. It tests no extrapolation, compute allocation, architecture shape, or language-model downstream predictability. It uses three model sizes (10M/40M/200M) and one seed. The result is a monotonic performance-vs-size trend in an RL setting. This is related to, but not, any version: V5 needs the power-law form and V6 concerns language-model downstream tasks. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that performance improves with larger models and that rapid fine-tuning works, mirroring language and vision trends, with DT scaling best. They report that TD methods (CQL) show no or 'inverse' scaling, attributed to instability. They caution that results are Atari-specific and that dataset scale and diversity may not suffice for NLP-like scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Measures Atari decision-making scores for offline RL agents rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy; no power-law fit or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by method: DT performance increases with model size, while other methods saturate or grow more slowly; CQL fine-tuning is inconsistent and drops sharply at larger sizes. Fine-tuning results use 1% of data from five held-out games.

fits_no_version.finding: Multi-Game Decision Transformer IQM human-normalized Atari score rises reliably from 10M to 200M parameters. BC grows more slowly or saturates; CQL does not improve (Fig. 5a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In offline multi-game RL, sequence-model (DT) agents' task performance increases monotonically with parameter count, while TD-based agents do not scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning score on 5 held-out games improves with DT size but drops sharply for larger CQL models (Fig. 5b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transfer performance after pretraining scales with model size for supervised sequence-model agents but shows inverse scaling for TD-learning agents.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger DT models reach higher game scores per training step (tokens seen) on Asterix and Seaquest (Fig. 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger sequence-model RL agents are more sample-efficient per token, as reported for language models.

record.problems: Scaling plots provide no numeric point values in the text. The authors evaluated only one training seed for most experiments, and explicitly caution against generalizing beyond Atari and aligned action/observation spaces.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. Results comparing methods on aggregate scores without a model-size or training-progress scaling condition were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters vs data.
Depth and width co-vary with size (Table 1); no fixed-size shape comparison.
RL setting, but no power-law form of loss or performance is tested; only a monotonic trend over 3 sizes.
No language-model downstream tasks and no performance-vs-pretraining-loss relation.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: UDRL (Impala) performance across ~5M/30M/60M sizes vs DT and CQL (Fig. 10, Fig. 13), another RL size-scaling result
missing.locator: Appendix D, Figure 10; Appendix E, Figure 13

missing.what: Seed variance for DT-40M: IQM 0.95 ± 0.05 over 5 seeds, used to judge size differences

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V6 and labelled them, but the study measures RL game scores over three sizes with one seed and no power-law or loss analysis. The 'downstream tasks' here are not language-model downstream tasks, so labels are dropped. All values are figure-only. Per-size rows add little; the trend is the result.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy or loss-versus-parameters, tokens, or compute measurements.
No power-law fits from small runs or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or comparison of parameter and token growth.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count for loss.
The study is in reinforcement learning, but measures Atari task performance rather than whether a power-law form holds for loss in another modality or training regime.
Tests Atari in-game scores against model size and training progress; does not test downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or other downstream task families.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, and no analysis of departures from a single loss power law.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Decision Transformer fine-tuning on five held-out Atari games
reader_labels.reason: The paper states that fine-tuning performance improves as the DT model gets larger; supported by r8.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Behavioral cloning and CQL on the 41 training games
reader_labels.reason: The paper says other methods saturate or grow much more slowly, and specifically that CQL does not improve with size; supported by r4–r7.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: CQL fine-tuning on five held-out Atari games
reader_labels.reason: Larger CQL models show a reported sharp performance drop, contrary to predictable improvement with scale; supported by r9.

reader_labels.label: supports
